turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Contemptuously, you say? Pray, enlighten me, Mr. Darcy. Do you presume to possess a complete understanding of Mr. Wickham’s misfortunes, and the character of those who have inflicted them?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Madam, I possess a knowledge of Mr. Wickham’s character that extends far beyond your amiable, and regrettably uninformed, sympathies. His misfortunes, as you term them, are largely self-inflicted, a consequence of a lifetime of deceit and reckless abandon.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: So, I am 'regrettably uninformed,' am I? It seems your pronouncements on others' characters are as boundless as they are ill-founded. Pray, Mr. Darcy, enlighten me further – what other depths of supposed depravity have you unearthed with your relentless scrutiny?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your impertinence, Miss Bennet, is truly remarkable. To suggest I delight in 'unearthing depravity' is a gross misrepresentation of my concern for truth and propriety – qualities, I fear, you seem to undervalue.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Truth and propriety, Mr. Darcy? You cloak your judgments in such lofty terms, yet they reek of arrogant presumption. I daresay, your 'concern' for propriety is merely a convenient excuse to indulge in your own self-righteousness.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I find myself compelled, Miss Bennet, to address a matter of considerably greater import than the petty grievances you seem so eager to dwell upon. Allow me, therefore, to state, with utmost sincerity and despite the evident displeasure it may cause you, that I am deeply, irrevocably in love with you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Love? From *you*, Mr. Darcy? It is a jest, surely, a particularly cruel one given the recent unpleasantness of your accusations. Do you imagine flattery, however clumsily delivered, will erase the memory of your interference in my sister’s happiness and your slanderous remarks about my family?

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I confess, the manner of my declaration was… perhaps less than ideal, given the circumstances. However, to dismiss it as a 'jest' or attribute it to a desire for 'flattery' demonstrates a profound misunderstanding, not only of my sentiments but of the depth of my regard for you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Deep regard? You presume much, Mr. Darcy. To declare such feelings after the manner you have, and with the history between us, smacks not of sincerity, but of a desperate attempt to justify past wrongs.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your accusations sting, though I confess, I anticipated little less. I do not seek to justify past actions, but to explain the principles which guided them; principles which, I now recognize, were tragically misapplied, and which nevertheless stem from a sincere desire to act with honour and protect those I deem worthy.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Honour? Protecting those you deem worthy? It appears your definition of honour involves manipulating lives and disparaging families, Mr. Darcy. Pray tell, which aspects of my family are so desperately in need of your 'protection' that warranted such interference?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You speak of principles, Mr. Darcy, as if they were some immutable laws, excuses for your meddling. But what principles dictate the right to dictate another's happiness, or to judge a family's character based on superficial observations? I find your justifications as tiresome as your initial arrogance.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your words are a relentless assault, and I confess, the vehemence with which you accuse me is… unsettling. However, to permit yourself such liberties without acknowledging the genuine concern that motivated my actions—a concern, I assure you, stemming from a profound sense of duty—is to deny the very possibility of rectitude in another’s conduct.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Duty? Rectitude? You cloak your interference in such lofty terms, Mr. Darcy, as if it somehow absolves you of responsibility for the pain you have caused. I daresay, if you possessed a modicum of genuine compassion, you would see the absurdity of attempting to justify actions born of pride and prejudice.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I am not attempting to *absolve* myself, merely to illuminate the reasoning behind my conduct, however flawed its execution. Your accusations, though delivered with considerable force, neglect to consider the genuine distress I experienced observing a union I believed would lead to irreparable harm – a concern that, I now concede, was coloured by my own presumptions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Irreparable harm? You presume to know what constitutes irreparable harm in another's life, Mr. Darcy? It seems your 'concern' was merely a convenient excuse to exert your influence, to impose your will upon those less fortunate – or, as you evidently perceive it, less *deserving*.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, you twist my words with a skill that is, I must admit, quite remarkable, though I find the purpose of such dexterity deeply regrettable. To suggest I derive satisfaction from imposing my will—a most unjust and offensive accusation—is to fundamentally misunderstand the burden of responsibility that accompanies my station and, indeed, my conscience. I confess, I sought to protect, and in so doing, erred grievously; but to characterize my actions as malicious is a distortion I cannot permit to stand unchallenged.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Malicious? Perhaps that is overly dramatic, Mr. Darcy, though your interference certainly *felt* malicious at the time. But to deny the arrogance inherent in believing you possess the wisdom to dictate another's happiness is a failing far more substantial than any perceived distortion I might commit.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your assessment is... pointed. While I acknowledge the validity of your observations regarding my perceived arrogance—a trait I am, admittedly, endeavouring to mitigate—to suggest I *dictate* another’s happiness betrays a profound misunderstanding of my intentions, and, dare I say, a significant degree of personal animosity.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Animosity, Mr. Darcy? I assure you, my feelings towards you are driven by a sense of justice, not personal spite. It is tiresome to be lectured on one’s understanding of your intentions when your actions themselves speak so loudly of a condescending disregard for the feelings of others.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: She answered him with cold civility.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His sense of her inferiority, of its being a degradation, of the family obstacles which judgment had always opposed to inclination, were dwelt on with a warmth which seemed due to the consequence he was wounding, but was very unlikely to recommend his suit.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: He concluded with representing to her the strength of that attachment which in spite of all his endeavours he had found impossible to conquer; and with expressing his hope that it would now be rewarded by her acceptance of his hand.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! repeated Darcy, contemptuously--yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
